chiefComplaint: Productive cough, fever & pleuritic chest pain — 4 days

history.lifestyle: Sedentary; limited physical activity due to shift work.

complaint.timeline: Gradual onset, worsening over the last 48 hours

interview.text: Hello Robert, I'm Aura, an AI assistant helping Dr. Nolan prepare for your visit. I'd like to ask a few questions about your symptoms. Can you describe the cough you've been having?
It started as a dry cough but for the last two days I've been bringing up thick phlegm. It looks kind of rusty-brown.
Thank you. Rust-colored sputum is useful information. Are you experiencing any chest pain, and if so, does anything make it worse?
Yes, a sharp pain on the right side of my chest. It gets much worse when I take a deep breath or cough.
That sharp pain worsening with breathing is called pleuritic pain. Have you had a fever or chills?
I had shaking chills two nights ago and my thermometer read 38.7. I feel hot and worn out.
Are you more short of breath than usual — for example, climbing stairs or walking to the car?
Definitely. Walking across the warehouse leaves me winded, which never used to happen.
Have you noticed any leg swelling, calf pain, or recent long travel or immobilization?
No swelling or calf pain. No long trips — I have been at work every day.
Understood — that helps me weigh a blood clot as less likely. Last question: are you keeping up with fluids, and how is your appetite?
Appetite is poor and I feel a bit dehydrated. I've been drinking water but not much.
Thank you, Robert. I have enough to prepare a structured summary for Dr. Nolan. Please rest — the care team will see you shortly.

summary.chiefComplaint: 58-year-old male with 4 days of productive cough, fever, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain, now with exertional dyspnea.
summary.hpi: Symptoms began 4 days ago with a dry cough that became productive of rust-colored sputum over the last 48 hours. Reports rigors with a documented temperature of 38.7°C, progressive pleuritic right-sided chest pain, and new exertional breathlessness. No hemoptysis, leg swelling, or calf pain. Poor oral intake with mild dehydration.
findings: Likely focal consolidation given rust-colored sputum & pleuritic pain
Diabetes raises risk of atypical/severe course

diagnoses.name: Community-acquired Pneumonia
diagnoses.tagline: Right lower lobe bacterial pneumonia, likely S. pneumoniae
diagnoses.reasoning: The constellation of fever with rigors, productive rust-colored sputum, pleuritic pain, focal right-lower-zone crackles with bronchial breathing, and hypoxia is highly characteristic of a lobar bacterial pneumonia. Rust-colored sputum is a classic descriptor for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Diabetes and age increase both likelihood and severity.
contradicting: No prior imaging yet to confirm consolidation
CRP/WBC pending at time of assessment
diagnoses.confidenceExplanation: Confidence is weighted from the strength of matching clinical features. Rust-colored sputum (+18), focal auscultation findings (+22), fever/rigors (+14), hypoxia (+12), and host risk (+8) contribute positively. The absence of confirmatory imaging and inflammatory markers currently caps the ceiling.
diagnoses.whyNot100: Imaging has not yet confirmed a consolidation, and a small subset of pneumonia mimics (e.g., pulmonary infarction from PE, aspiration) can present similarly. Confidence will rise to ~95% once a chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation and inflammatory markers are elevated.
diagnoses.riskAssessment: CURB-65 ≈ 1–2 (RR 24, age 58). Borderline hypoxia in a diabetic host warrants close monitoring; consider short-stay observation rather than immediate discharge.
diagnoses.nextAction: Order a chest X-ray and CBC/CRP now. If consolidation is confirmed, start empiric non-penicillin antibiotics (penicillin allergy) — e.g. respiratory fluoroquinolone or macrolide + cephalosporin per local guidance.

references.title: ATS/IDSA Guideline on Community-acquired Pneumonia in Adults

references.snippet: Recommends chest imaging plus clinical criteria for diagnosis and CURB-65/PSI for severity stratification.

references.title: Value of sputum color in predicting bacterial etiology of lower respiratory infection
references.snippet: Purulent, rust-tinged sputum showed higher positive predictive value for bacterial pneumonia.

references.title: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch. 121 — Pneumonia
references.snippet: Classic lobar pneumonia from S. pneumoniae presents with rigors, pleuritic pain and rusty sputum.

similarCases.title: 55 M, ex-smoker, lobar pneumonia

discussion.text: The distinguishing features are the focal signs and hypoxia. Acute bronchitis rarely produces localized bronchial breathing over a single lobe, and it does not usually cause an SpO₂ of 92% or a respiratory rate of 24. Combined with rigors and rusty sputum, this points to alveolar consolidation rather than airway-limited inflammation. A chest X-ray will settle it — I'd expect a lobar infiltrate.

diagnoses.name: Pulmonary Embolism
diagnoses.tagline: Considered due to pleuritic pain, dyspnea & hypoxia
diagnoses.reasoning: PE can present with pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea and hypoxia, which overlap with this case. However, the febrile course with rigors, productive rusty sputum and focal auscultation findings favor infection. No DVT signs, no immobilization, and no tachy-arrhythmia lower the pre-test probability.
contradicting: High fever with rigors (atypical for PE)
missing: CT pulmonary angiogram if D-Dimer positive
diagnoses.confidenceExplanation: A low Wells score, absence of DVT risk factors, and a strongly infective picture pull confidence down. Hypoxia and pleuritic pain keep PE on the differential but as a secondary consideration.
diagnoses.whyNot100: PE cannot be fully excluded on clinical grounds alone in a hypoxic patient; a negative D-Dimer would effectively rule it out given the low pre-test probability.
diagnoses.riskAssessment: Wells score ≈ 1.5 (tachycardia). Low probability — D-Dimer is an appropriate rule-out test.
diagnoses.nextAction: Send a D-Dimer alongside the septic workup. A negative result in this low-probability patient safely excludes PE without CT radiation.

references.title: ESC Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Management of Acute PE
references.snippet: Recommends Wells/Geneva scoring and D-Dimer for low/intermediate probability patients before imaging.

references.title: Fever in acute pulmonary embolism
references.snippet: High-grade fever with rigors is uncommon in PE and should prompt a search for infection.

similarCases.title: 59 M, pleuritic pain, hypoxia
similarCases.detail: Low Wells score; infection ultimately confirmed on imaging.

discussion.text: Why not pulmonary embolism? He is hypoxic.

Hypoxia is shared by both, so it doesn't discriminate. What tips me away from PE is the combination that PE rarely explains: a temperature of 38.7°C with rigors, rust-colored purulent sputum, and focal bronchial breathing over one lobe. His Wells score is about 1.5 and he has no DVT signs or immobilization. That said, I wouldn't dismiss it — a D-Dimer is cheap and, if negative, safely closes the door on PE here.

diagnoses.name: Acute Heart Failure
diagnoses.tagline: Dyspnea in a hypertensive patient — lower likelihood
diagnoses.reasoning: Hypertension and dyspnea raise heart failure as a possibility, but the febrile, focal, and productive-cough picture is not typical. No orthopnea history, no peripheral edema, normal heart sounds without a gallop, and a clear cardiac exam make decompensated heart failure unlikely as the primary driver.
diagnoses.confidenceExplanation: Confidence is low because the cardinal features of decompensated heart failure (bilateral crackles, gallop, edema, orthopnea) are absent, and an infective explanation is much stronger.
diagnoses.whyNot100: Not applicable — heart failure is a low-probability contributor. A normal NT-proBNP would effectively exclude it.
diagnoses.riskAssessment: Low probability. Worth a single NT-proBNP to exclude given the hypertensive history and tachycardia.
diagnoses.nextAction: Add NT-proBNP and ECG to the panel; no further cardiac workup unless BNP is elevated.

references.title: ESC Guidelines for Heart Failure
references.snippet: Natriuretic peptides recommended to rule out heart failure in patients presenting with dyspnea.

similarCases.title: 63 M, dyspnea + HTN
similarCases.detail: Dyspnea attributed to respiratory infection after negative cardiac workup.

discussion.text: What finding would change your confidence in heart failure?

The single most decisive input would be NT-proBNP. A clearly elevated level (e.g. > 900 pg/mL for his age) plus an S3 gallop, bilateral basal crackles and peripheral edema would move heart failure up substantially. Right now every one of those cardinal signs is absent, which is why I have it at 22%. A normal BNP would let me effectively rule it out.

summary.chiefComplaint: 24-year-old female with 16 hours of periumbilical pain that migrated to the right lower quadrant, with nausea and anorexia.
summary.hpi: Classic migratory pain beginning periumbilically and localizing to McBurney’s point. Associated anorexia, nausea and low-grade fever. Pain worsens with movement and coughing (suggesting peritoneal irritation). LMP one week ago, on OCP — pregnancy unlikely.

exams.reason: Retrocecal appendix irritation of psoas muscle.

diagnoses.name: Acute Appendicitis
diagnoses.reasoning: Textbook migratory pain to McBurney point with anorexia, nausea, low-grade fever, guarding, positive Rovsing and rebound. Alvarado score of 8 places this at high probability. Ultrasound/CT will confirm and exclude perforation.
diagnoses.confidenceExplanation: Alvarado score 8/10 (migration +1, anorexia +1, nausea +1, RLQ tenderness +2, rebound +1, fever +1, leukocytosis pending). High clinical probability drives confidence to 88%.
diagnoses.whyNot100: Imaging confirmation and a white cell count are still pending. A normal appendix on a good-quality ultrasound would substantially lower confidence.
diagnoses.riskAssessment: High risk of progression to perforation if delayed > 24–48h. Surgical review should not wait for all results.
diagnoses.nextAction: Keep nil-by-mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, urgent surgical consult, and expedite ultrasound + bloods.

references.title: World Society of Emergency Surgery — Jerusalem Guidelines for Acute Appendicitis
references.snippet: Recommends Alvarado/AIR scoring with imaging to reduce negative appendectomy rate.

references.title: Diagnostic accuracy of the Alvarado score

discussion.text: What test should I order first?

A urine β-hCG first — it is fast and rules out ectopic pregnancy, which is the can’t-miss mimic in a woman of this age. Then a CBC/CRP and a graded-compression ultrasound of the RLQ. In parallel, I would not delay the surgical consult; an Alvarado of 8 warrants review regardless of imaging turnaround.

diagnoses.name: Ovarian Torsion / Cyst
diagnoses.reasoning: Right adnexal pathology can mimic appendicitis. However, the classic migratory pattern and GI symptoms favor appendicitis. Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler will assess adnexae and blood flow.

diagnoses.confidenceExplanation: Kept on the differential because of sex and pain location, but the migratory GI-predominant picture is atypical for torsion.
diagnoses.whyNot100: Torsion is a surgical emergency that imaging must exclude; a normal Doppler flow lowers it further.
diagnoses.riskAssessment: Moderate — torsion threatens ovarian viability, so imaging should assess adnexal flow.
diagnoses.nextAction: Ensure the ultrasound request explicitly includes pelvic views with Doppler.

summary.chiefComplaint: 71-year-old female with 1 week of progressive dyspnea, orthopnea (4 pillows), PND, bilateral ankle edema and 3 kg weight gain.
summary.hpi: Progressive congestive symptoms over one week on a background of ischemic cardiomyopathy, AF and CKD. Orthopnea, PND and peripheral edema with rapid weight gain point to fluid overload. Notably lapsed her furosemide for several days — a common precipitant of decompensation.

diagnoses.name: Decompensated Heart Failure
diagnoses.reasoning: The congestive syndrome — orthopnea, PND, raised JVP, bibasal crackles, S3 gallop, peripheral edema and rapid weight gain — on a background of ischemic cardiomyopathy is diagnostic of decompensated heart failure. A lapsed diuretic is the likely trigger. NT-proBNP and echo will confirm and grade severity.
diagnoses.confidenceExplanation: Multiple cardinal congestive signs each add substantial weight (JVP +16, S3 +14, orthopnea/PND +18, edema +12, weight gain +10). Pending BNP/echo currently caps confidence at 86%.

discussion.text: Could this be a COPD exacerbation instead?

It is worth considering, but several features point away from airways disease: she has orthopnea and PND, an S3 gallop, a raised JVP and pitting edema — all congestive signs rather than bronchospasm. She is an ex-smoker without a documented COPD diagnosis or wheeze. If the chest X-ray shows interstitial edema and NT-proBNP is high, heart failure is confirmed. I would still auscultate for wheeze and check the CXR for hyperinflation to be thorough.

diagnoses.riskAssessment: Low–moderate; treat the dominant cardiac process first.
diagnoses.nextAction: CXR to distinguish congestion from hyperinflation.

discussion.text: The most valuable input would be spirometry showing reversible airflow obstruction — a ≥ 12% and 200 mL improvement in FEV1 after salbutamol would be near-confirmatory and push confidence above 90%. recommendedTests: Usually clinical — imaging only if red flags

discussion.text: Any safety concern I should act on now?

diagnoses.tagline: New diagnosis confirmed on HbA1c & fasting glucose

If he fails to respond to oral therapy or the picture shifts, antibody (GAD) and C-peptide testing would clarify, but nothing here suggests that is necessary.

diagnoses.name: Left Ureteric Stone (Renal Colic)
diagnoses.tagline: 5 mm stone at left vesicoureteric junction on CT KUB
diagnoses.reasoning: Textbook renal colic — sudden severe unilateral loin-to-groin pain with restlessness and visible hematuria in a patient with a prior identical stone. CT KUB confirmed a 5 mm stone at the left VUJ with mild proximal hydronephrosis and no infection.
contradicting: Must always exclude AAA in older patients (here low risk, age 38)
diagnoses.confidenceExplanation: CT KUB is the gold standard and directly visualized the stone, so confidence is very high. Clinical features and hematuria were already strongly supportive pre-imaging.
diagnoses.whyNot100: Imaging is essentially confirmatory; the small residual accounts for always ensuring no coexisting infection or obstruction requiring urgent drainage.
diagnoses.riskAssessment: A 5 mm stone has a good chance of spontaneous passage. Key safety issue — exclude infection (none here); an infected obstructed kidney would be a urological emergency.
diagnoses.nextAction: Analgesia (NSAID first-line), antiemetic, hydration and medical expulsive therapy (alpha-blocker). Stone under 6 mm — trial of passage with urology follow-up and stone-prevention advice.

discussion.text: Does a 5 mm stone need intervention?

Usually not first-line. Stones under 6 mm have roughly a 60–70% chance of passing spontaneously, so the guideline-preferred approach is medical expulsive therapy with an alpha-blocker, good analgesia and hydration, plus a safety net. Intervention (e.g. ureteroscopy or lithotripsy) is reserved for failure to pass, uncontrolled pain, or signs of infection/obstruction — none of which are present here.
